title: Umbria
quiz.0.question: What was Umbria's first DOCG?
quiz.0.explanation: Torgiano Rosso Riserva was originally part of Torgiano, Umbria's first DOC (1968), and became Umbria's first DOCG in 1990; Montefalco Sagrantino followed in 1992.
quiz.1.question: How is Montefalco Sagrantino Passito made?
quiz.1.explanation: For the Passito, the grapes are dried (appassimento) for at least 2 months before fermentation and the wine is aged at least 37 months (no mandatory wood) — Sagrantino's traditional style.
quiz.2.question: Which grapes are the basis of Orvieto DOC?
quiz.2.explanation: Orvieto requires at least 60% Grechetto and/or Procanico (Trebbiano Toscano), typically blended with Malvasia Bianca Lunga, Verdello and Drupeggio.
quiz.3.question: What is the main difference between Montefalco Rosso and Sagrantino di Montefalco?
quiz.3.options.1: Rosso is a Sangiovese + Sagrantino blend
quiz.3.explanation: Montefalco Rosso is Sangiovese-led (60–80%) with 10–25% Sagrantino and at least 18 months of ageing; Montefalco Sagrantino DOCG is 100% Sagrantino aged 37 months.

slides.1.title: 💚 Italy's Green Heart
slides.1.content:
Umbria is the only landlocked region of central and southern Italy and Italy's hilliest region, known as "the green heart of Italy" (Cuore Verde d'Italia).

Umbria is famous for Montefalco Sagrantino (one of Italy's most tannic reds) and Orvieto whites.

slides.3.title: 🍇 Sagrantino — Italy's King of Tannin
slides.3.content:
💪 One of Italy's most tannic grapes

Sagrantino is Umbria's signature red grape: thick-skinned, very high in polyphenols, powerful and with remarkable ageing potential. Historically it was made mainly into a sweet passito, and it was almost extinct by the 1960s.

Montefalco Sagrantino DOCG

Location: Montefalco and 4 surrounding villages

Grape: 100% Sagrantino

Style: dark ruby, powerful, tannic, full-bodied, high in alcohol

Flavours: black cherry, blackberry, plum, leather, chocolate, game, spice

Ageing rule: min. 37 months (12 in wood)

Ageing potential: 15–30 years
slides.4.title: 🍷 Sagrantino's Two Styles
slides.4.content:
🍇 Montefalco Sagrantino (Secco)

Dry

Style: mainstream since the mid-1980s

Winemaking: min. 37 months of ageing (12 in wood); "secco" need not appear on the label

Tannins: extremely high and firm, softened by age

Alcohol: 14–16%

Flavours: black fruit, leather, tobacco, chocolate, spice

Pairing: game (wild boar, venison), grilled red meat, aged Pecorino

Drinking window: 5–10 years after vintage, can age 30 years

🍇 Montefalco Sagrantino Passito

Sweet

Style: the ancient traditional version

Winemaking: grapes dried (appassimento) before fermentation

Drying: min. 2 months

Ageing: min. 37 months (no mandatory wood)

Flavours: dried fruit, fig, dark chocolate, coffee, liquorice, raisin

Pairing: chocolate desserts, blue cheese, nut tarts

Hallmark: Sagrantino's traditional style, sweetness and earthiness balanced by tannin (the name is said to come from sacro, "sacred")
slides.5.title: ⚪ Orvieto DOC — Umbria's Classic White
slides.5.content:
🏰 The white-wine tradition of Orvieto

Orvieto is Umbria's largest, most productive and most exported DOC, with a history going back to the Etruscans (8th century BC).

🍇 Grapes

  • Grechetto and/or Procanico (Trebbiano Toscano) at least 60% combined
  • Typical partners: Malvasia Bianca Lunga, Verdello, Drupeggio
  • A white-only appellation shared by Umbria and Lazio, with most of the area and output in Umbria

🍷 Styles

Secco (dry): the mainstream style

Flavours: white flowers, green apple, almond, minerals

Style: fresh, medium-bodied

Abboccato (off-dry): the traditional style

Flavours: honey, apricot, white flowers

Residual sugar: 10–30 g/L

Classico: the historic core, higher quality

Superiore: stricter rules

Sweet: Vendemmia Tardiva (late harvest) and Muffa Nobile (noble rot) — Orvieto is one of the few places in Italy where noble rot develops on the vine

🍽️ Pairing

  • 🐟 Freshwater fish (Umbria's rivers and lakes)
  • 🍝 Spaghetti carbonara
  • 🍄 Truffle dishes (Umbrian black truffle)
  • 🧀 Fresh cheeses

slides.7.content:
🍇 Sagrantino's "little brother"

Montefalco Rosso is a Sangiovese + Sagrantino blend, easier to drink and more affordable than Sagrantino di Montefalco — the entry point to Montefalco's terroir. Montefalco DOC also includes Montefalco Bianco (min. 50% Trebbiano Spoletino) and Montefalco Grechetto (min. 85% Grechetto).

slides.8.title: 🍇 Other Umbrian Wines
slides.8.content:
Torgiano Rosso Riserva DOCG

Location: Torgiano, near Perugia

Grape: min. 70% Sangiovese

Style: elegant, well structured, good ageing potential

Hallmark: Umbria's first DOCG (1990), its rules modelled on Lungarotti's Vigna Monticchio

Ageing: min. 3 years

Grechetto (varietal wine)

Grape: Grechetto (100%)

Two Grechettos: Grechetto di Orvieto (Umbria's traditional white grape — light, citrusy and crisp, also late-harvest or botrytised) and Grechetto di Todi (= Pignoletto, native to Emilia-Romagna — full-bodied with firm acidity); they are not genetically identical

slides.9.title: 📜 Umbria's Appellations Explained (IWS Official Material)
slides.9.content:
🏺 Torgiano Rosso Riserva DOCG

Giorgio Lungarotti: one of the most important figures of the post-war Italian wine industry; he launched Rubesco in 1962 and drove the creation of Umbria's first DOC, Torgiano (1968).

Rules: originally part of Torgiano DOC, it became a separate DOCG in 1990 — Umbria's first; closely modelled on Lungarotti's Vigna Monticchio; min. 70% Sangiovese and min. 3 years of ageing.

🍇 Montefalco Sagrantino DOCG & Montefalco DOC

Area: both share the same boundaries — Montefalco and 4 other villages; continental climate on the western foothills of the Central Apennines, 220–450 m; soils mainly lacustrine deposits of yellow sand and sandy clay.

DOCG: both versions must be 100% Sagrantino. The dry wine needs min. 37 months of ageing (12 in wood) — dark ruby, powerful, tannic, full-bodied, high in alcohol and long-lived; the Passito needs min. 2 months of drying and 37 months of ageing (no mandatory wood), its sweetness and earthiness balanced by tannin.

Three DOC categories: Montefalco Rosso (Sangiovese 60–80%, Sagrantino 10–25%, other reds max. 30%, min. 18 months; Riserva 30 months incl. 12 in wood), Montefalco Bianco (min. 50% Trebbiano Spoletino), Montefalco Grechetto (min. 85%).

⚪ Orvieto DOC

History: a prestigious wine area since Etruscan times, prized by the Romans and favoured by the papacy in the Middle Ages; the traditional style was golden, prickly and soft-sweet, and the abboccato style lasted into the 1950s before drier wines took over in the second half of the 20th century. Delimited in 1931; when the DOC was created in 1971 the area was extended and the original zone named Classico.

Area: hills around Orvieto at 100–500 m, influenced by the Tevere and Paglia rivers and Lakes Bolsena and Corbara — one of the few places in Italy where noble rot develops on the vine.

Rules: a white-wine appellation shared by Umbria and Lazio; at least 60% Grechetto and/or Procanico (Trebbiano Toscano), typically with Malvasia Bianca Lunga, Verdello and Drupeggio; a Classico sub-zone, a stricter Superiore, and two sweet styles, Vendemmia Tardiva and Muffa Nobile.

🌿 Colli Martani, Spoleto, Todi and Umbria IGT

Colli Martani DOC: overlaps Montefalco and parts of Todi and Spoleto; the home of Grechetto, plus Trebbiano Toscano, Sangiovese, Vernaccia Nera and international grapes such as Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay and Sauvignon. Two sub-zones: Grechetto di Todi and Vernaccia di Cannara (passito).

Spoleto DOC (2011): created to promote Trebbiano Spoletino, overlapping the eastern parts of Colli Martani and Montefalco; Bianco min. 50% Trebbiano Spoletino, varietal Trebbiano Spoletino min. 85%.

Umbria IGT: covers the whole region with a wide range of styles and quality; excellent Grechetto, Trebbiano Spoletino, Ciliegiolo, Sangiovese, Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon are made under it.

slides.11.title: 🏛️ History and Heritage
slides.11.content:
⏳ From the Etruscans to Lungarotti and Caprai: Orvieto has been a famous wine since antiquity and Montefalco was known for sweet Sagrantino; in the second half of the 20th century two key figures put Umbria on the international stage.

Antiquity

🏺 Etruscans and Romans

  • Orvieto: a renowned wine area since Etruscan times, prized by the ancient Romans
  • Traditional viticulture: vines trained up trees (alberata) and grown among other crops (coltura promiscua)
Middle Ages

⛪ The papacy and Montefalco

  • Orvieto: favoured by the papacy; the traditional style — golden, prickly and soft-sweet (abboccato) — lasted into the 1950s
  • Montefalco: a known wine area since the 11th century, where Sagrantino was made mainly as a sweet passito
Early 20th c.

📜 Rules and change

  • 1920s: first official appearance of dry Sagrantino
  • 1931: Orvieto officially delimited
  • 1950s–60s: few Sagrantino vineyards remained; in the second half of the century Orvieto turned drier
Modern revival

🚀 Lungarotti, the DOCs and Caprai

  • 1962: Giorgio Lungarotti launches Rubesco, laying the foundations of modern Umbrian viticulture and winemaking
  • 1968: Torgiano becomes Umbria's first DOC; in 1971 Orvieto DOC is created, extended beyond its historic area, which is named Classico
  • 1979: Montefalco DOC created; dry Sagrantino becomes mainstream by the mid-1980s
  • 1990 / 1992: Torgiano Rosso Riserva becomes Umbria's first DOCG; Sagrantino di Montefalco is elevated to DOCG
  • 1990s: Arnaldo Caprai drives Sagrantino's explosion in popularity; Spoleto DOC (2011) promotes Trebbiano Spoletino, saved by Cantina Novelli
slides.12.title: 🌍 Topography, Climate and Soils (IWS Official Material)
slides.12.content:
🏔️ Italy's hilliest region: its inland position and altitude create a transition from a Mediterranean climate in the west to a continental one in the east, moderated by Lake Trasimeno and the Tevere.

⛰️

Topography and climate

  • Mountains: the Central Apennines in the east, the Sub-Apennines (Subappennini) in the west and the Monti Martani in the centre
  • Water: the Tevere (Tiber) runs through the region; Lake Trasimeno lies in the west
  • Climate: shaped by the inland position and altitude, shifting from Mediterranean in the west to continental in the east; moderated by Lake Trasimeno and the Tevere
🪨

Soils

  • Centre: alluvial and lacustrine deposits from the ancient Lake Tiberino
  • South-west: sand, gravel and clay of marine origin
  • Northern half: sandstone, marl and clay
  • Around Orvieto: volcanic soils (tufo, basalt, pyroclastic debris)

slides.13.title: 🍇 Umbria's Grapes Explained (IWS Official Material)
slides.13.content:
🔴 Red grapes

Sangiovese

  • Umbria's most widely planted grape (about 20%), considered traditional
  • Made as a varietal or blended with Sagrantino, Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon
  • The backbone of Torgiano Rosso Riserva and Montefalco Rosso

Sagrantino

  • Umbria's signature red grape, native here
  • Thick-skinned and high in polyphenols; historically used for sweet passito
  • Almost extinct by the 1960s, revived by dry Sagrantino

⚪ White grapes

Grechetto di Orvieto

Umbria's traditional white grape

Light, citrusy and crisp; also late-harvest or botrytised; the backbone of Orvieto

Grechetto di Todi

= Pignoletto / Grechetto Gentile

Native to Emilia-Romagna; full-bodied with firm acidity, also used for sparkling wine; Todi, Colli Martani, Montefalco

Trebbiano Spoletino

Native to Umbria

Almost extinct in the 20th century, saved by Cantina Novelli; refreshing acidity, medium to full body; Spoleto DOC, Montefalco Bianco DOC, Umbria IGT

⚠️ Grechetto di Orvieto and Grechetto di Todi are not genetically identical. In Umbria, Procanico is Trebbiano Toscano.

🌍 International varieties

PointDetail
ShareAbout 20% of plantings
DevelopmentWidely adopted in the 1980s–90s; most Umbrian DOCs allow international grapes as varietals or blend components
Most plantedMerlot is the most widely planted international grape, followed by Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc
TrendInterest has now shifted back to native and traditional grapes

🍇 Other local grapes

🔴 Ciliegiolo

  • A frequent source of fine Umbria IGT wines

🔴 Gamay del Trasimeno

  • Despite the name, a biotype of Cannonau (Grenache)

🔴 Vernaccia Nera

  • Used for passito in Colli Martani's Vernaccia di Cannara sub-zone
slides.14.title: 🍷 The Evolution of Winemaking
slides.14.content:
⚗️ From tradition to modernity — a revolution in tannin management: in the 1980s–90s Arnaldo Caprai led a winemaking revolution, turning Sagrantino from rustic and wild into powerful and elegant.

🏺 Traditional methods (1950–1980)

  • Vessels: large Slavonian oak casks (botti) of 5,000–10,000 L, 20–50 years old, with almost no oak flavour
  • Maceration: 30–40 days → over-extraction, coarse and bitter tannins
  • Ageing: 3–5 years in large casks, slow oxidation, a very long wait before drinking
  • Fining and filtration: little or none, cloudy wines with heavy sediment
  • Style: wild and rustic, sandpaper tannins, needing 20–30 years; inconsistent quality

🔬 Modern methods (1990–today)

  • Vessels: temperature-controlled stainless steel + French barriques (225 L), 26–28°C, micro-oxygenation
  • Maceration: 20–25 days, controlled, with délestage (rack-and-return) 2–3 times a day for gentle extraction
  • Ageing: 12–18 months in French barriques + 6–12 months in large casks, 30–50% new oak
  • Tannin polymerisation: micro-oxygenation speeds tannin–anthocyanin bonding; drinkable after 5–8 years
  • Style: elegant, balanced, silky tannins, enjoyable at 5–10 years, with 20–30 years of potential

🍇 Traditional passito drying

1️⃣
Harvest and selection

Hand-picked in mid-October, choosing perfect bunches

→
2️⃣
Drying

At least 2 months on cane mats or wooden racks

→
3️⃣
Weight loss

Water evaporates, concentrating sugar and flavour

→
4️⃣
Fermentation and ageing

Slow fermentation leaving residual sugar; min. 37 months of ageing (no mandatory wood)

slides.15.title: 🗺️ The Montefalco Zone and Its Wines
slides.15.content:
🍇 Montefalco and 4 surrounding villages: Montefalco Sagrantino DOCG and Montefalco DOC share exactly the same boundaries, on the western foothills of the Central Apennines at 220–450 m.

⛰️ Montefalco

Role: the heart of the zone, called "the balcony of Umbria"

Soils: lacustrine yellow sand and sandy clay

Significance: the historic centre of Sagrantino, a known wine area since the 11th century

Key producers: Arnaldo Caprai, Paolo Bea, Antonelli, Scacciadiavoli

🏛️ Bevagna

Location: north-west of Montefalco

Terrain: gentler hills and valley land

Significance: one of the zone's 5 villages

Key producer: Adanti (Arquata)

🌬️ Gualdo Cattaneo

Location: west of Montefalco

Terrain: hills

Significance: one of the zone's 5 villages

Note: the hilly country west of Montefalco

🌾 Giano dell’Umbria & Castel Ritaldi

Location: south and south-west of Montefalco

Terrain: hills

Significance: the zone's other 2 villages

Note: together with Montefalco, Bevagna and Gualdo Cattaneo they make up the 5 villages

Italian law has no cru classification for Montefalco, but top producers label wines by single vineyard or flagship name.

slides.18.questions.0.question: What was Umbria's first DOCG?
slides.18.questions.0.explanation: Torgiano Rosso Riserva was originally part of Torgiano, Umbria's first DOC (1968), and became Umbria's first DOCG in 1990; Montefalco Sagrantino followed in 1992.
slides.18.questions.1.question: How is Sagrantino di Montefalco Passito made?
slides.18.questions.1.explanation: For the Passito, the grapes are dried (appassimento) for at least 2 months before fermentation and the wine is aged at least 37 months (no mandatory wood) — Sagrantino's traditional style.
slides.18.questions.2.question: Which grapes are the basis of Orvieto DOC?
slides.18.questions.2.explanation: Orvieto requires at least 60% Grechetto and/or Procanico (Trebbiano Toscano), typically blended with Malvasia Bianca Lunga, Verdello and Drupeggio.

slides.18.questions.3.options.1: Rosso is a Sangiovese + Sagrantino blend

slides.18.questions.4.options.1: B. Very high tannin and ageing potential

slides.18.questions.5.question: In Umbria, Trebbiano Toscano is also known as…
slides.18.questions.5.explanation: In Umbria (especially Orvieto) Trebbiano Toscano is called Procanico; Trebbiano Spoletino is a different native Umbrian grape, and Grechetto di Todi is Pignoletto.
slides.18.questions.6.question: Who laid the foundation of modern viticulture and enology in Umbria?
slides.18.questions.6.explanation: Giorgio Lungarotti was one of the most important figures of the post-war Italian wine industry: he launched Rubesco in 1962 and drove Torgiano to become Umbria's first DOC in 1968. Arnaldo Caprai later drove Sagrantino's popularity in the 1990s.
slides.18.questions.7.question: Vines in Umbria were historically trained using…
slides.18.questions.7.explanation: Umbrian vines were traditionally trained up trees (alberata) among other crops (coltura promiscua); the alberello bush vine is not an Umbrian tradition.
slides.18.questions.8.question: What are the main grape varieties of Colli Martani DOC?
slides.18.questions.8.explanation: Colli Martani is the home of Grechetto, along with Trebbiano Toscano and Sangiovese (plus Vernaccia Nera and international grapes); its sub-zones are Grechetto di Todi and Vernaccia di Cannara.
slides.18.questions.9.question: Which Umbrian appellation has conditions favourable to noble rot (muffa nobile)?
slides.18.questions.9.explanation: Influenced by the Tevere and Paglia rivers and Lakes Bolsena and Corbara, Orvieto is one of the few places in Italy where noble rot develops on the vine, and it has a Muffa Nobile sweet style.
